en: The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Teaching on the Precepts for Eliminating Calamities, one fascicle;
translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty].
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a certain district where all [the people] were devoted to...
The people practiced the Buddha’s five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, so that within the entire jurisdiction of the county, there was no one who brewed alcohol.
Among them was the son of a prominent family who wished to travel far away for trade; as he was about to depart, his parents said to him:
"Be diligent in observing the five precepts and practice the ten wholesome actions; take care not to drink wine and violate the grave precepts of the Buddha."
Having received these instructions, he set out.
Arriving in another country, he met former classmates and friends; they rejoiced upon seeing one another.
He took them back with him and produced grape wine, wishing to drink it together.
He replied, "In my country,
we revere the Buddha and observe the five precepts, with none daring to transgress them.
Those who drink alcohol are reborn as foolish people and do not encounter the Buddha."

Furthermore, when one takes leave of one's parents to travel, they offer mutual admonitions; yet to indulge in wine and thereby persistently violate their instructions and transgress the precepts constitutes a crime greater than any other.
Though my friends may feel joy at our long-awaited reunion after separation, they should not cause me to break the precepts and disobey the teachings of my parents.
The host said:
"I and you share the same teacher; in kindness we are brothers. To me, my parents are as your own; since our parents hold one another in such high esteem, how could I possibly go against this?"
"If I were in your house, I would surely comply with your son's wishes.
Having no other recourse, he finally consented to drink it.
He lay drunk for three days; upon waking, his heart was filled with regret and dread.
When the matter was concluded, he returned home and reported everything in detail to his parents. His parents replied:
"You have disobeyed our instructions and further violated the precepts; this is the beginning of the corruption of the Dharma, and you are no filial son."
"Do not speak of this; let it serve as a warning to the state.
He then took the items he had obtained and drove him out of the country, saying, "It is not fitting for you to remain here.
Because the son had violated the precepts, he was expelled by his own kin and went to another country, where he stayed at an inn.
The master served three spirits who were able to manifest as humans, appearing before him to eat and drink and conversing with him.

The master served them for many years until he grew exhausted; his wealth was completely depleted, and illnesses and deaths never ceased in his household. Becoming weary and disgusted by these spirits, he discussed the matter privately with others.
The ghosts knew the man's thoughts and were distressed by them; they deliberated among themselves, saying:
"This man’s wealth has been exhausted entirely for our sake, yet it has never brought us any benefit, and thus we have come to loathe and suffer his presence."
"It would be fitting to seek out precious treasures to bestow upon him, so as to gladden his heart!
He then stole fine jewels from the treasuries of kings in other lands and piled them up in the garden, saying to the man:
"You have served me for many years with great diligence and toil; now I wish to bring you merit and make you wealthy—is this not a source of joy?"
The host said,
"I receive the great grace of the deity.
The ghost said:
"There is gold and silver within your garden; you may go and take it. This will bring you great merit and fulfill your wishes.
The host, delighted, entered the garden and saw the extraordinary objects. He carried them back to his house on his back and, expressing his gratitude for the favor received, said:
"I wish to prepare a meal tomorrow; I pray that you would deign to grace us with your presence."
When the preparations of food and drink were all complete, the spirits arrived at the gate; seeing the people of Śrāvastī in the host’s house, they fled in haste.
The host called out after him, requesting he return, saying:
"I have now prepared this modest offering and everything is complete; since you, Great Deity, have already deigned to descend, why do you abandon it and depart?
The deity replied:
"You have entertained a venerable guest; how could I venture forward?
He fled again in alarm.
The host returned to his seat and reflected to himself:
"There is no one else in my house but this very person!
He immediately came out and spoke, respectfully providing whatever he had to offer, and they enjoyed themselves to the utmost.
When the meal was finished, he questioned him, saying:
"What merit have you accumulated in this world that my tutelary deity, whom I serve, should flee from you in fear?"
The guest explained in detail the Buddha’s merits, the five precepts, and the ten wholesome actions;

he confessed that although he had indeed violated the precept against alcohol, he had been driven out by his relatives because he still observed the remaining four precepts, and was thus protected by celestial deities whom your spirit dared not oppose.
The host said, "Although I have served this deity for a long time, I am weary of it; I now wish to uphold the Buddha’s five precepts.
Thereupon, he received from his guest the three refuges, the five precepts, and the ten wholesome actions, practicing with single-minded diligence and not daring to be indolent.
He asked where the Buddha was and whether it would be possible to see him.
The guest replied, "The Buddha is at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī; you may go there and see him."
The host traveled with single-minded focus until he reached a pavilion.
Inside was a woman of exquisite beauty, who was actually the wife of a man-eating demon.
Having traveled a great distance, the man’s time was pressing as evening approached; he asked the woman for lodging for one night, and she replied:
"Be careful not to remain here; you should depart immediately.
The man asked, "For what reason?
Is there some intention behind this?"
The woman replied, "I have already spoken to you; why do you ask again?
The man thought to himself:
"The people of Śrāvastī in the past observed the Buddha’s four precepts in their entirety, yet my spirit was still so terrified by them.
I have now received the three refuges, the five precepts, and the ten wholesome actions; with a mind free from indolence, what have I to fear?"
He then remained there to stay the night.
A man-eating ghost, seeing the majestic power of his observance of the precepts, hovered by his side for forty *li* from the pavilion; having stayed there one night, it did not return.

The next day, as the man was proceeding on his journey, he saw the scattered remains of human skeletons being devoured by ghosts; his hair stood on end and his heart was filled with fear and regret. He withdrew to reflect:

"In my own country, my home life provided me with every necessity and comfort in abundance. Yet, having been deceived by this man who said the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, I have seen nothing marvelous, but instead find these skeletons strewn about."
Evil thoughts arose once more, and he thought to himself:
"It would not be better to return that woman to her native land and dwell together with her as before; would that not be pleasant?"
He immediately turned back and returned to the pavilion; following the woman there, he again requested to stay the night.
The woman said to the man, "Why have you come back?"
He replied, "My plans did not succeed, so I have returned; I shall stay for one more night.
The woman said:
"You are doomed to die!
My husband is a man-eating ghost and will arrive before long; you must leave at once. This man did not believe her and stopped, refusing to go.

His mind became even more deluded, and his lustful desires arose again. No longer did he have faith in the virtue of the Triple Refuge of the Buddha, nor the mind of the Five Precepts and Ten Wholesome Actions. Consequently, the celestial deity departed and no longer protected him.
When the ghost returned, the woman, fearing that the ghost would devour the man, took pity on him and hid him inside a jar.
Hearing the scent of human breath, the ghost said to the woman:
"Have you obtained some meat?"
"I wish to eat it.
The wife said, "I will not go; how could I obtain meat?"
The wife asked the ghost,
"Why did you not return last night?
The ghost replied:
"Because you sat while neglecting a noble guest and allowing him to stay overnight, I have been driven away.
The man inside the jar became even more terrified; he no longer recognized the meaning of the Three Refuges.
The wife asked,
"Why did you not obtain meat?
The ghost replied:

"It is precisely because you have expelled my disciple from the Buddha's community that a celestial deity drove me forty *li* away. Forced to sleep in the open air, I am trembling with fear and remain uneasy even now; therefore, I could not obtain any meat."
Upon hearing this, the wife was silent with joy and asked her husband, "What are the Buddha's precepts?
How shall we fully observe and uphold them?
The ghost replied:
"I am extremely hungry and have come in haste with this meat; you need not ask about it.
This is the unsurpassed, truly correct precept, which is not something I dare to speak of."
The wife said, "Tell me about it, and I shall give you some meat.
The ghost, being greedy and cruel, desired to eat without restraint; pressed by the wife’s questioning, he then proceeded to recite for her the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts:
First, to be compassionate and benevolent, refraining from killing;
second, to maintain pure faith, refraining from stealing;
third, to preserve chastity, refraining from sexual misconduct.
The fourth was to refrain from idle speech;
the fifth was to be filial and obedient and not to drink to intoxication.

When the ghost first proclaimed the first precept, the woman immediately accepted it. She held the five precepts in her heart and recited them aloud; the man, having recognized the five precepts within the jar, accepted them accordingly.
Śakra, Lord of Devas, knowing that these two people had taken refuge in the Buddha in their hearts, immediately selected fifty benevolent deities to protect them, whereupon the ghost fled.
On the following day, the wife asked the man, "Were you afraid?"
He replied:
"Great is my fear!
By the grace of your benevolence, my mind has awakened and I have recognized the Buddha."
The wife asked the man,
"Why did you return yesterday?
He replied:
"I saw the skeletons of people who had died long ago scattered about; because I was terrified by them, I bent down and turned back.
The woman said, "Those bones were ones I myself had discarded."
"I was originally a daughter of a noble family, but was abducted by a ghost who took me as his wife; I am miserable and destitute, with no one to whom I may appeal.
Now, having received your benevolent grace, I have been able to hear the Buddha's precepts and am freed from this ghost."
The woman asked,
"Virtuous one, where do you intend to go now?
The man replied:
"I wish to go to the kingdom of Śrāvastī to see the Buddha.
His wife said,
"Excellent!"
"I shall leave my native land and my parents to follow the worthy one and see the Buddha.
They then proceeded forward together.
On the way, they encountered four hundred and ninety-eight people, with whom they exchanged greetings.
“Virtuous ones!
From where have you come, and where do you wish to go?
They replied:
"We have come from the presence of the Buddha.
They asked,
"Since you have already seen the Buddha, why do you go back again?"
He replied, "The Buddha, the Sun, preached the sutras, but my mind was bewildered and I could not yet understand; now I am returning to my own country.

The two sages recounted the beginning and end of the matter in detail. Because ghosts fear those of high conduct who observe the precepts, their minds were then opened and enlightened, and they both returned together to see the Buddha.
The Buddha saw him from afar and smiled; five-colored light issued forth from his mouth.
Ānanda knelt down and said, "The Buddha does not smile without cause; there must be something he intends to say."
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Do you see these four hundred and ninety-eight people or not?
He replied:
“I see them. The Buddha said, “These four hundred and ninety-eight people have now found their original teacher; those who come to see the Buddha shall all attain the Way.”

The five hundred people went before the Buddha, prostrated themselves in worship, and listened to the sutra with single-minded devotion. Their minds were opened and their understanding attained; they all became śramaṇas and realized the path of arhatship.
The Buddha said:
"The one who violated the precept against alcohol was the innkeeper, who had been a brother to this woman for successive lifetimes;
furthermore, these two were the teachers of four hundred and ninety-eight people in their previous lives."
"When people of the world seek the Way, they must obtain a true teacher and virtuous friends; only then will they attain understanding.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, all the bhikṣus were greatly rejoiced; they came forward to pay homage to the Buddha and departed.
The Scripture on the Buddha’s Teaching on the Precepts for Eliminating Calamities, one fascicle.
